scenes.title: Validation starts with uncertainty
scenes.visual: Founder reviews an anonymous Discover decision record.
scenes.narration: Welcome to Validate. Discover helped you define a problem and opportunity. Validation now means gathering evidence about important assumptions to inform a decision. It is not a badge that proves a whole business will succeed. Start with your Discover choice and unresolved questions.

scenes.title: Name a claim that could be wrong
scenes.narration: Choose one specific assumption about the problem, proposed benefit, behaviour or possible payment. People understand my idea is different from people will use or pay for it. State the group and context. If your Discover decision was refine or pause, respect that choice before planning further tests.

scenes.title: Match evidence to the claim
scenes.visual: Editable reported account, observed action and commitment cards.
scenes.narration: A recent-experience account may inform the problem. An observed action may inform behaviour in a setting. A specific commitment may inform a next step, but its meaning depends on the conditions. No single kind of evidence proves every claim. A polite compliment or clarity check is not purchasing evidence.

scenes.title: Design a bounded check
scenes.visual: Founder prepares a small permission-based test plan.
scenes.narration: Choose a small check suited to the question. State what it can and cannot tell you, what might support or weaken the assumption, and how you will record results. Do not invent a passing threshold or assume a few convenient participants represent everyone. Keep plans separate from findings.

scenes.title: Respect constraints and negative results
scenes.visual: Editable permission, privacy and reconsideration cards.
scenes.narration: Permission, voluntary participation and privacy still matter. Do not collect money, contact participants or launch a test merely because a worksheet is complete. A negative or ambiguous result can help you refine, repeat or pause. Define the next decision before defending your idea.

scenes.title: Create your validation starting brief
scenes.narration: Build your Validation Starting Brief. Record the handoff, group, priority assumption, question, proposed method, signals, constraints and review plan. This is a plan for learning, not evidence collected or a validated venture. Next you will identify and prioritise the assumptions that matter most.

sections.label: 02 / LEARN
sections.heading: Match evidence to a specific claim.

children: Validation
means gathering evidence about assumptions to inform a decision. An
assumption
is a claim that could be wrong. A
test
is a bounded way to investigate it. A
signal
is information you will interpret with its context and limitations.
Problem
Recent-experience accounts and permitted observation can inform whether a difficulty occurs and matters in a context.
Benefit / clarity
Understanding a benefit statement can indicate clarity. It does not prove adoption or payment.
Behaviour / commitment
Observe a relevant action or specific commitment under clear conditions. Preserve what it does and does not establish.
Payment
Payment assumptions require their own suitable evidence. No money is collected or payment test executed here.
Illustrative example:
a visitor says directions sound helpful. That is a reported reaction, not proof they will change behaviour or pay. Ask what claim you are checking before choosing a method.
Review the Discover go/refine/pause decision.
Name one specific assumption for a group/context.
Choose a fitting small check and its limitations.
State supporting and weakening signals without invented thresholds.
Set permission, privacy, owner, timing and review decision.
Negative or ambiguous results can justify refine, repeat or pause. Convenient participants are not automatically representative. A plan or completed lesson is not findings.
